title: What 'sealed' means
description:
A sealed record exists but the public cannot see it: a judge or a statute has closed it. Sealing differs from destruction (expungement) and from redaction (partial release) — the record survives, intact, behind a legal wall.

This database documents the wall itself — what was public, when it closed, and why — using only public sources. It never reproduces the sealed contents.

title: Grand jury secrecy (Rule 6(e))
description:
Federal grand jury proceedings are secret by law — witnesses, votes, and deliberations. The secrecy protects the innocent accused and encourages candid testimony. What the grand jury was, when it met, and whether it indicted are typically public; what happened inside is not.

This record documents the secrecy rule itself — a public law creating a private space.

description:

Dozens of states have expanded expungement in recent years — a public policy shift toward second chances.

description:

The 72-year rule is the rare case where private becomes public on a published timetable.

Public applications becoming secret by law: the reverse of the patent bargain.

The privilege's use — and abuse — is documented in public case law.
